div.p: This paper presents a new assignment and scheduling technique for Hardware/Software partitioning in realtime embedded systems. In contrast to previous approaches, resource constraints are taken into account as soon as possible in order to reduce both the blocking time and the schedulability loss due to resource contention.

The system is composed of an arbitrary number of tasks with hard real-time deadlines and different periods. Our method provides the assignment and the scheduling to hardware/software components for each sub-task of each task. Results show that our approach works for cases which cannot be dealt with other methods.

div.head: Introduction
div.p: Embedded real-time systems are getting more and more commonplace in our daily life. Today, such systems can be found in all cars, planes, cellular phones, cameras... Furthermore, since these systems are getting more and more intricate, they are often multiprocessor systems. To make the trade-off between performance and overall costs, they require both hardware and software components. So, the system's architectural definition requires simultaneous synthesis of hardware and software architectures. This problem is commonly referred to as hardware-software cosynthesis. Hardware-software co-synthesis involves various steps such as allocation, assignment, scheduling, and performance estimation. Allocation determines the number and the type of all the hardware/software components. Assignment maps all tasks (or sub-tasks in our approach) of the specification to these components. Scheduling determines both the sequencing of tasks mapped to a component and the sequencing of communications on a link.

In addition to processing units, a task may require other resources for its execution. By resources, we will specifically mean passive resources. Examples of such resources are memory, mutexes and database locks. Resource contention affects the execution behavior and the schedulability of the tasks. If the memory bus of an embedded system is a bottleneck, how memory is assigned and memory access is scheduled has a predominant influence on overall performances.

In this paper, we consider a static assignment and scheduling of periodic tasks for hardware/software embedded systems with resource constraint to reduce the undesirable effects of resource contention. Our goal is to minimize the schedulability loss due to blocking. Blocking occurs when a priority inversion makes a higher priority task waiting for the processing of a lower priority task.

We propose a method which deals with resource constraint for heterogeneous hard real-time systems and which tries to minimize the blocking time. Blocking time is the third term of the following well known relationship [1]:

Since the scheduling and the assignment problems are interdependent, we reduce their complexity by first assigning -for each task -the sub-tasks on a Processing Unit (PU) in order to bind resources on PUs and to minimize the schedulability loss due to blocking. Then, we perform the Priority-Ceiling Protocol [2] (PCP) with the Rate Monotonic scheduling [3] (RM) at the task level in order to reduce the blocking time and avoid deadlock.
In contrast to previous approaches, resource constraints are taken into account as soon as possible in order to reduce the schedulability loss due to resource contention.

This paper is organized as follow. Section 2 reviews previous works related to co-synthesis and existing scheduling techniques for periodic tasks that target distributed heterogeneous architectures. Section 3 describes the model we use to describe the system. Section 4 gives a motivating example. Our algorithms are described in Section 5. Section 6 gives examples and test cases. The last section concludes the article.

div.head: Related Work
div.p: Hardware/software co-synthesis is the study of the design of systems containing both hardware and software components which satisfy constraints such as cost, timing and so on. It has been an important area of research [4]. Many papers have been published, which differ by both the architectures targeted and the algorithms used. Some of them target one-CPU/one-ASIC architectures [5][6] [7] and some others target n-CPU/m-ASIC architectures [8][9][10] [11]. In fact, for any given architecture, there is a vast amount of literature devoted to the scheduling in real-time systems. [12] and [13] give a good introduction to scheduling techniques used in heterogeneous real-time systems.

Most of these works consider the data dependencies in periodic or/and aperiodic task graph models [8][9] [11]. Definition of a task graph will be given in the next section. Some scheduling techniques handle the control dependencies in the task graph model [14] [15]. The algorithm presented in this paper targets periodic task graphs without control dependency information.

Since none of previously referenced articles handles explicitly the sharing of common resources and since they schedule sub-tasks independently each others, we want to take into account the effect of blocking caused by the need for synchronization of tasks that share a common resource. Because the problem of deciding the feasibility of the scheduling with resource sharing is NP-hard [16], heuristic approaches are widely used to generate feasible scheduling [17]. In the monoprocessor context, a control protocol, called Priority Ceiling Protocol (PCP), has been proposed [2] to bind the priority inversion to avoid deadlock problems and to limit the time a higher priority task waits a resource to be free. This protocol has been generalized, and also includes remote blocking, in the context of shared memory multi-processor [12]. Nevertheless, these techniques address only scheduling for heterogeneous hard real-time systems and none of them address the assignment problem.

It is known that the class of algorithms covered by static approaches is restricted because it forbids conditional and data-dependent iterations. But, such algorithms are widely used in signal processing context and, furthermore, a self-timed strategy allows broadening the class of the algorithms covered by our approach [18]. Section 5 will describe our heuristic to solve assignment and scheduling problems.
In the next section, we describe the models used in this article. Then we present a simple example to show the performance limitations of some previous works [4] [19] [20].

div.head: Models
div.p: The specification of the problem is composed of three components: a task graph, a processor graph and a technology description.

div.head: Task Graph Figure 1. Task Graph
div.p: A task graph is a collection of periodicals tasks. Each task is represented by a DAG -Directed Acyclic Graph which root identifies the initiation point for the task. Other nodes (also called actors in DFG -Dataflow Graph terminology) represent subtasks or critical sections. Note that as in DFG, edges represent data dependencies so that, on a given edge, sink actor can compute only if source actor has completed his own computing. Task graph also indicates for each task the period and the deadline of the task. Numbers on edges represent the amount of data to transfer between PUs when source actor is computed on another PU than sink actor. As the data uses the communication channel, these values take into account the speed of the interprocessing unit communication (details are given in next section). Let us consider the example given in Figure 1. The task T 1 (resp. T 2 ) has a period equal to 10 (resp. 20) and a deadline of 8 (resp. 20). The starting point of each task is represented by a black circle and shaded subtasks represent the utilization of a given resource R by the sub-task.

div.head: Processor hyper graph
div.p: The target architecture is described by a hyper graph. Nodes represent PUs (DSP, ASIC ...) and edges represent communication channels. Communication channels can be connected to several PUs. Edges are valuated to specify the communication time spent to transfer each data unit between PUs.

div.head: Technology description
div.p: The PU technology description specifies how fast each sub-task runs on each type of PU and the resources needed by each sub-task. Intuitively, the use of the infinite symbol would forbid the execution of a sub-task on a PU.

div.head: Figure 4. Assignment of R on PU 1
div.p: Figure 5 shows how our method differs from previous approach. In fact, previous approach first assign tasks independently each others and then compute a method (here we use PCP) to allocate all the tasks to the same hardware/software system while minimizing the blocking times. But, blocking times introduced by PCP can make our assignment overlap its hard real-time constraints. Our method takes the blocking times into account at the assignment phase. Results show that our approach works for cases which cannot be dealt with other methods.

div.head: Assignment steps
div.p: In this section, we describe the heuristic (given in Algorithm 1) we develop to solve the assignment step.

div.p: A list T of n periodic preemptible tasks partially specified, T = {(C 1 , P 1 , D 1 )… (C n , P n , D n )}, ordered by decreasing periodic task values. Values for C i will be fixed at the assignment step.

A set P of m processors, P = {PU 1 , PU 2 … PU m }. Note that the resource priority is given by the maximum priority of the tasks which use it. Now, we will describe the two main steps of our heuristic.

div.head: Selection phase
div.p: During this phase, we perform RMS and PCP [2] at a task level [19] for all assignments given in the previous phase. RMS is performed by using the task's computation time estimation computed during the assignment phase.

div.head: Assignment phase
div.p: Algorithm 3 presents a heuristic so that the schedulability loss due to blocking is minimal. Before presenting this heuristic, we need to introduce three terms. In the next tree sub-sections, we will use the following notations: E(T i , PU j ) denotes the execution time of the subtask T i on the PU j, E * (T i ) is the median of all E(T i , PU j ). If the median is infinite, E * (T i ) is the higher finite value of E(T i , PU j ), d(T i , PU j ) is the difference between E(T i , PU j ) and E * (T i ), DA(T i , PU j ) is the earliest time at which all data required by sub-task T i is available on the PU j, SL(T i ) is the static level of the sub-task T i . Its value is equal to the longest path containing T i computed by using E * (T i ) values, TF(PU j ) represents the time at which the last subtask assigned to the PU j finishes its execution, TS(T i , PU j ) denotes the time at which the sub-task T i begins its execution on the PU j. Note that as TF(PU j ) depends on previous sub-tasks, its value should be computed in a recursive fashion.

div.head: Examples and test cases
div.p: This section explains why previous approaches are insufficient. First, we illustrate our heuristic by an example. Then we show that our method deals with cases that traditional methods don't. Finally we compare our algorithm's performances with others algorithm's performances.

div.head: Illustration
div.p: To illustrate our heuristic assignment, we'll study the task graphs T 1 and T 2 given in Figure 1. We recall that the architectural description is given in Figure 2 and the task description is given in Table 1. We assume that T 1 (witch have a greater priority than T 2 ) is already assigned and the resource R is allocated to PU 2 . So, the assignment heuristic will run in six steps (one by subtask) successively. Figure 6 shows the result of our heuristic's computation. The main important point to retain is that, in order to avoid the blocking in time 11 of Figure 3, our heuristic inserts an idle time after the sub-task h.
The benefits of this idle time is that the RMS is performed without blocking time and so, none of the tasks overlaps it's deadline.
This example shows that, even if we constrain assignment of R on PU 2 , our heuristic is able to find a correct solution that others methods don't.

div.head: Experimental results
div.p: In this section, we give some examples to analyze our heuristic's performance compared with other heuristics. We have implemented our heuristic in JAVA. Comparison results are given in Table 2. We have to modify algorithms given in [9] [11][14] in order to impose that sub-tasks sharing a common resource have to be implemented on the same PU. Our algorithm reduces the schedulability loss of an average of 12%. Otherwise, for more than 10%, our method works for cases which didn't be dealt with other methods.

div.head: Conclusions
div.p: In this paper, we have addressed the problem of scheduling and assignment for hardware/software embedded real-time systems with resource contention. Our goal has been to minimize the schedulability loss due to blocking. Since the scheduling and the assignment problems are interdependent, we reduce their complexity by first assigning, for each task, the Assignment phase Estimate all capacity of all tasks For each sub-task T i

For each PU PU j Compute DL, DB, DLB End For Select max DLB End For Return (Assignment) End sub-tasks on a processing unit, then performing the priority-ceiling protocol [2] with the rate monotonic scheduling [3]. We have represented the system by an acyclic task graph with different hard real-time deadlines and periods.
We use this algorithm as a component in a cosynthesis methodology for systems implemented on heterogeneous multi-processors.
